newsitem.title: UK: French truck dispute becomes focus for UK air mart.
newsitem.headline: French truck dispute becomes focus for UK air mart.

text.p: The focus of attention in the UK air cargo market has swung away from arguing about the rights and wrongs of surcharges to focus instead on the chaos created by the French truck driver strike and frantic efforts to switch cargoes to air, a Reuter survey showed.

The underlying market continued to be active and seasonally firm as air will soon be the only freight option for items needing to reach their destination before Christmas which is now less than four weeks.
"General activity is ahead of last year but has not quite reached the level of clamour we saw in 1994," said the sales manager of one airline.

The tightening grip of the French trucking dispute on shipments to and from the UK has been worsened by the closure of the Channel tunnel following last week's fire. In addition a Danish trucking dispute reduced the options available to forwarders and shippers trying to avoid existing bottlenecks.
As a result "every spare kilo of capacity is being used' said a manager of one airline specialising in freighter leasing.

Much of the European airfreight market is in fact a trucked one and forwarders and airlines said the apparent contradiction of just what airfreight really means in Europe, has been underlined over the past ten days.

From a fairly early stage of the French dispute shippers and forwarders who normally use trucks to send so-called air freight through channel ports to and from northern France had begun to seek alternatives using Belgian and Dutch ports.

But despite the somewhat overheated demand this created for genuine space on aircraft, forwarders and airlines said that intercontinental rates had not really risen as the spot market was very small with regular customers taking nearly all available space.
There may have been many more enquiries but there simply was not capacity to satisfy the demand, airlines and agents said.
Firms who do not normally use space on aircraft are suffering most and are having to wait for what little spare capacity might exist.

The demand for aircraft capacity has pushed rates for chartering aircraft higher and air brokers said one would probably pay around 1,000 stg a tonne or 1.00 to 1.50 a kilo to fly manufactured parts or fresh produce inside Europe.

Another source at a charter airline said firms wanting to hire planes are probably having to pay 700 stg a tonne but stressed the difficult of naming a rate owing to widely different volume to weight ration such as between lettuces and different loading and loading rates.
Another cargo agent said that depending on the plane it would probably costs some $30,000 to $40,000 to fly fresh produce from Spain to northern Europe.

Planes have flown Spain to the UK and to Germany with fresh fruit and vegetables and brokers said it would be logical to expect other exporters such as Israel to try and take advantage of the disruption exports being trucked through Spain.

Although car manufactures will have had contingency plans in case of road blockages they will still need to charter aircraft if component stocks run low and threaten assembly plants with shutdowns. The same is true for high-tech industries where the cost of assembly disruption to high value goods means they willing to pay expensive charter rates.

UN agencies flying relief aid to Rwanda who had pre-booked flights are not really competing with this sudden rush of commercial demand and thus are not in the same category of just-in-time chartering.
Former large Soviet Antonov and Ilyushin military transport planes are widely used for aid flights and have been used this week to fly fresh produce into the U.K. and northern Europe.

Airlines in the charter business said they have limited ability to satisfy sudden demand as they should have forward bookings for their planes and not have to rely on sudden panic demand such as was created this week.
Airlines will serve their regular customers first and with much European truck and ferry traffic brought to a halt there simply was not enough capacity to satisfy demand.

Some airlines brought in additional capacity from the U.S.. and Emery drafted in a two DC10 freighters from the U.S. as well as increasing the flights flown by a European based DC8, said Mike Rawlings, Emery sales manager for Europe, the Middle East and Africa.
This has not stopped at least two of Britain's largest supermarket chains from chartering planes to fly fruit and vegetables from Spain.

J. Sainbury Plc chartered a Russian owned Ilushin 76 to fly 40 tonnes of oranges from Valencia in Spain with another flight scheduled for Thursday. Rival chain Tesco Plc has also admitted flying in afresh food from Spain to London's main airports.
Motor and other manufacturers faced disruption to assembly lines from a shortage of components made in different countries but normally trucked to a single assembly plant.
Cargo managers said firms like Ford or General Motors are obvious examples of multinationals with dispersed component plants.

Airlines contacted in the survey said most forwarders and shippers now accepted the need for airlines to be compensated for higher fuel costs but equally said they understood that the way they had been introduced had not been well received.

Deviants from the surcharge are Japan Airlines(JAL) and All Nippon Airlines who increasing rates by six pence a kilo instead of imposing surcharges as the former does not require approval by Japan's Civil Aviation Bureau (JCAB).

The still strong level of business and the forward demand already reaching into December probably means an extension of the seasonal rush will extend to close to Christmas and already some airline cargo managers are talking of the strong market continuing into January.
JAL's Tony Edwards said there the east bound market was very strong with demand for cargo space for electrical goods, pharmaceuticals and chemicals and this had meant "rates were very hard".
All Nippon's John O'Shea said demand was holding up very well and featured big shipments of CD's and electronics.
A new competitor for space on eastbound flights has come from some of the "pop" alcopop" soft drinks which are attracting a new market in the far east, cargo manager said.

Rates on most long distance flights were little altered from the last survey but airline cargo managers said a different approach on surcharges further clouded the issue with two Japanese airlines this week increasing rates instead of imposing surcharges.
Airlines operating on other Asian routes also reported a level of business with no real sign yet of momentum dropping off before Christmas.
British Midland Airways has not imposed a surcharge but did increase rates by some 2.5 percent at its last review in October, cargo general manager Terry Greetham told Reuters.
British Midland specialises in carrying express traffic and thus has avoided much of the commotion surrounding the French trucker strike.

British Midland offers door-to-door services to Paris and Brussels of under five hours and flies as far as Prague and may extend further afield where air has a clearer time advantage over high speed trains, he added. -- Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
